before: This calculator compares hosting costs per productive kWh. It adds management and power-factor percentages to the advertised rate, then divides by the share of hours when machines run. It then divides by one minus the pool-fee fraction. The result is an equivalent cost for comparison, not an actual invoice or profit calculation.
after: This calculator converts a hosting rate into an equivalent cost per productive kWh. It adds separately billed fees to the rate. When stopped hours remain payable, the same cost is spread over fewer productive hours. The pool’s revenue deduction is then expressed as a cost adjustment.
note: States what is calculated first, without repeating the full worked arithmetic in the introduction. The steps retain the additive fee rule, productive-hours divisor and pool divisor (E24, E25, E28).

before: Use this if you own machines and pay for booked hosting capacity even when the machines are stopped. Hosting businesses can use it for machines they own. Energy-only billing, revenue-share contracts, demand-response income and unrelated hosting income need different models.
after: Use this for machines you own when booked capacity remains payable during downtime or curtailment. Energy-only billing, revenue-share contracts, demand-response income and unrelated hosting income need different models.
note: Keeps the paid-capacity condition and all excluded business models. Machines owned by a hosting business fit the same ownership condition without a separate role sentence (E24, E28).

before: Check the agreement and invoices. Which fees are included in the advertised rate, and do you still pay when machines stop?
Enter Advertised power rate in $/kWh. Enter management and power-factor fees as percentages of that rate. Do not add a fee already included in the rate.
Enter downtime and curtailment as percentages of the same period. Use records or clearly labelled assumptions. Count each stopped hour once, under one input only.
Enter Pool fee as a percentage of revenue. The tool converts it to an equivalent cost for comparison; it is not an electricity charge.
Compare each step and the final rates using the same assumptions for both offers. A smaller percentage increase can still leave you with a higher final cost.
Copy the URL to save the inputs. Anyone with the link can read the terms you entered.
after: Check the agreement and invoices. Which fees are included in the advertised rate, and do you still pay when machines stop?
Enter Advertised power rate in $/kWh. Enter management and power-factor fees as percentages of that rate. Do not add a fee already included in the rate.
Enter downtime and curtailment as percentages of the same period. Use records or clearly labelled assumptions. Count each stopped hour once, under one input only.
Enter Pool fee as a percentage of revenue. The tool converts it to an equivalent cost for comparison; it is not an electricity charge.
Compare the final rates using the same billing assumptions for both offers.
Copy the URL to save the inputs. Anyone with the link can read the terms you entered.
note: Keeps checking agreements, separate additive fee inputs, distinct paid lost hours, pool revenue deduction and public-URL warning. Moves the percentage-versus-final-rate interpretation to its result explanation, where it is needed (E24, E25).

before: This shows how your inputs change the starting rate. It does not rate the provider’s honesty or quality.
after: Compare the final $/kWh rates as well as the percentage increases. A lower percentage increase can still leave a higher final cost.
note: Explains how to use the result. Removes the unrelated detour about judging provider honesty or quality while preserving the material comparison caveat (E24, E28).

before: Use the working to check the arithmetic and compare assumptions. The model does not recommend a provider.
after: The change at each step shows how much that adjustment adds to the starting rate.
note: Explains the intermediate calculation instead of disclaiming a provider recommendation. Keeps the arithmetic and the equivalent-cost boundary elsewhere (E24, E28).

before: Booked capacity is assumed payable during lost hours. Credits, energy-only charges, curtailment compensation and revenue-share contracts need separate treatment.
The pool-fee calculation is an equivalent comparison adjustment, not the actual dollar charge a pool takes from revenue. Mining revenue is not an input.
The model does not include BTC price, difficulty, machine efficiency, hardware cost, repairs, financing, tax, deposits or resale value. It cannot determine profitability.
Management and power-factor percentages add once. Compounded charges or fees applied to a different base need separate arithmetic.
The defaults and presets are illustrative. No market rates, provider ranking or safe decision threshold are established here.
